This paper integrates system dynamics and evolutionary game theory, defines the behavioral characteristics and core objectives of the three parties, constructs a multi-agent evolutionary game model under digital supervision scenarios, designs a payoff matrix and replication dynamic equation, and analyzes the impact mechanism of key parameters on the evolution of the parties' strategies through system dynamics simulation, identifying the evolutionary stable strategy of the supervision system. The results show that improved efficiency of digital supervision and optimized reward and punishment mechanisms can effectively promote the three parties towards a benign equilibrium of "strict government supervision - active enterprise management - strict supervision by the supervisor,"providing theoretical support and decision-making reference for optimizing the digital supervision system of High-risk sub-projects. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Suppressing Hallucinations in Anti-Fraud LLM Agents: The Robust Dual-Verification (RDV) Architecture
authors: Huo, Menghao; Xue, Zhiming; Lu, Kuan; Yan, Weiran
venue: 2026 10th International Conference on Electronic Information Technology and Computer Engineering, EITCE 2026
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in financial anti-fraud systems are susceptible to hallucinations that manifest as numerical drift, fabricated entity relations, and logic overstepping of compliance rules. These errors carry severe regulatory and financial consequences. This paper proposes the Robust Dual-Verification (RDV) architecture, a multi-layered framework designed to suppress hallucinations in anti-fraud LLM agents. RDV integrates four synergistic components: A Structured-Semantic Retrieval-Augmented Generation mechanism (S2-RAG) enforcing Text-To-SQL anchoring and row-level citation tracing; a LoRA fine-Tuning strategy targeting JSON schema compliance; a Dual-Agent Debate Protocol governed by a logistic calibration model for log-odds fusion; and deterministic guardrails providing a final hard-verification layer for explicit numerical claims. We introduce a domain-specific hallucination taxonomy and the Financial Adversarial Trap (FAT-1200) benchmark to rigorously evaluate the proposed architecture. Experiments demonstrate substantial reductions across all hallucination categories, with transparent evaluation methodology and honest discussion of practical limitations in real-world deployments. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Prediction-aided hierarchical and safe reinforcement learning for cold-chain electric vehicle routing
authors: Liu, Yangyang; Xu, Ying; Gong, Yitian; Zhang, Hao; Liu, Qingyun; Li, Zhiyuan; Wen, Yixun
venue: Energy
abstract: Cold-chain electric vehicle routing is a challenging problem in sustainable logistics because routing decisions must jointly consider traffic congestion, battery depletion, charging availability, refrigeration demand, thermal safety, and customer time windows. These tightly coupled factors make conventional static routing models inadequate, particularly in dynamic refrigerated distribution environments where future operating conditions and service risks must be anticipated. This paper proposes a Prediction-aided Hierarchical and Safe Reinforcement Learning (PHASE) framework for cold-chain electric vehicle routing. The proposed framework integrates prediction-aided state representation, hierarchical decision-making, and safety-oriented policy learning into a unified routing paradigm. By embedding future traffic, charging, and thermal information into the decision process, PHASE enables refrigerated electric vehicles to make forward-looking operational choices. The hierarchical structure distinguishes among service, charging, return, and protection behaviors, while the safety mechanism reduces infeasible actions caused by low state-of-charge, excessive cargo-temperature deviation, or severe service delay. The proposed framework improves the adaptability and robustness of routing policies under time-varying operating conditions and supports coordinated optimization of punctuality, energy efficiency, charging efficiency, and cold-chain safety. PHASE is particularly suitable for large-scale refrigerated logistics systems in which refrigeration energy consumption and spoilage risk must be explicitly incorporated into routing intelligence. The framework provides a scalable and practical solution for intelligent cold-chain electric distribution under complex dynamic constraints. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

title: Developing and Evaluating Ecologically Valid Study Tasks to Investigate Human-Robot Teaming
authors: Chadha, Jasmin Jaya; Pischulti, Patrick Kenneth; Hume, Ciara; Selleck, Zachary; Roessmann, William; Arquilla, Katya
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, HRI Companion 2026
abstract: Psychological safety, the shared belief held by team members that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, has been assessed in many human teams in the corporate workplace, yet it has not been analyzed to the same extent in complex environments or with multi-agent teams. Many studies have either evaluated team dynamics in human-robot interaction (HRI) completely in the wild or in highly controlled laboratory studies. This work presents operationally relevant study tasks that can be implemented in a controlled laboratory environment to characterize psychological safety in HRI. 33 participants completed 2 different tasks repeatedly with a human and robot teammate. We observed higher performance scores when participants worked with a human vs. a robot, suggesting that these tasks elicit differentiable performance responses based on team type that could be related to differences in psychological safety. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Optimization of DDPG positioning and navigation technology for warehouse logistics robots
authors: Zhou, Ximin
venue: Progress in Engineering Science
abstract: To address the core limitations of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithms in warehouse logistics robot navigation—specifically, inadequate temporal memory, inaccurate Q-value evaluation, and low training sample efficiency—this paper proposes a novel multidimensional optimization scheme. The main novelties include: (1) Integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks into the Actor-Critic framework to enhance historical state utilization and decision continuity; (2) Adopting an improved dueling network architecture to decouple the Q-value into state value and action advantage, thereby refining critic evaluation accuracy; and (3) Designing a dynamic dual-pool experience replay mechanism that prioritizes high-value samples based on TD-error and reward dimensions to optimize training efficiency. These three components form a synergistic optimization system. Experimental results demonstrate that the optimized algorithm significantly outperforms the original DDPG. It achieved a trajectory coherence index of 0.9 (a 38 % improvement) and an obstacle avoidance success rate of 83 %. The dueling network reduced the Q-value mean squared error to 2 × 10 −3 , while the dynamic dual-pool mechanism increased key sample utilization to 89.3 % and accelerated convergence speed by 38 %. In practical tests, the algorithm exhibited a dynamic obstacle avoidance response time of 210 ms, a path optimality index of 0.95, and a multi-robot task delay of only 5.2 s. The proposed multidimensional optimization strategy significantly enhances the adaptability, reliability, and navigation efficiency of warehouse logistics robots in complex dynamic environments, providing a robust solution for intelligent warehousing systems. Additionally, we discuss safety/ethical requirements and deployment scalability (compute and communication constraints) for large robot fleets. © 2026

title: Active Maritime Copilot for Ambiguity and Risk-Driven Decisions
authors: Lu, Zhichen; Stephenson, Matthew; Clement, Benoit; Tapus, Adriana
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, HRI Companion 2026
abstract: Cross-modal conflicts in maritime navigation-where a vessel’s verbal communication contradicts its physical maneuvers (e.g., promising to give way while maintaining speed) pose severe risks to safety. Current autonomous systems often process sensor data and linguistic inputs in isolation, failing to detect such discrepancies. We present a Multimodal Agentic Framework that serves as a “Watchful Copilot,” using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to cross-reference navigational dialogue with real-time kinematic data. To manage uncertainty, a Risk-Prioritized Interface employs progressive disclosure, escalating from a “Green” (Verified) state to a “Yellow” (Ambiguous) state, where the agent visualizes supporting evidence and requests human supervision for clarification. Preliminary validation in a 2D simulation benchmark (N = 13) provides initial evidence that this human-in-the-loop workflow may support reduced cognitive load and appropriate trust calibration in high-ambiguity scenarios, warranting further investigation. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Quad-Tree Based Collision Detection for Scalable Multi-robot Motion Planning
authors: Zaro, Abdel; Tajbakhsh, Ardalan; Johnson, Aaron M.
venue: Springer Proceedings in Advanced Robotics
abstract: This paper presents an efficient and scalable collision checking method for large multi-robot teams based on a quad-tree data structure. We introduce several key modifications to the original quad-tree including rules for handling collision checks near boundaries. In addition, we provide a thorough performance comparison against pairwise collision checking, bounding volume hierarchies (BVH), and other variations of quad-trees. The results indicate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms other baselines in terms of collision checking time for large number of robots. For a 200-robot test, our approach achieved a 2.8x speedup over BVH and an 11.8x speedup over pairwise, without missing any collisions. However, pairwise collision checking remains a reasonable approach for small numbers of robots due to the reduced setup time needed. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Agronomy-aware multi-robot path planning in hilly orchards via improved Beluga hierarchical optimization
authors: Wu, Zhengkai; Song, Juhui; Qian, Fei; Xie, Kai; Bao, Xiulan; Li, Shanjun
venue: Smart Agricultural Technology
abstract: Hilly citrus orchards feature narrow single-passage rows, elevation variation, heterogeneous vehicle loads, and soil that is sensitive to repeated traffic. These characteristics turn orchard coordination into a formation-aware, path-dependent multi-agent path-finding problem rather than a pure distance-minimization task. This paper proposes an Improved Beluga Hierarchical Guided Path Planning framework (IBHGPP). Each constraint-tree node maintains a shared weighted cell-entry map built from the current joint paths. During low-level replanning, partial operational benefit, marginal revisit risk, and task coverage are updated recursively for every candidate transition. A dual-key FOCAL strategy uses additive time and normalized mobility cost to define a bounded primary search range, while three agronomic terms determine the expansion order within that range. The five objective weights are calibrated off-line by an improved Beluga whale optimizer that combines Latin hypercube initialization, a cosine-decaying search coefficient, stagnation-triggered elite perturbation, early stopping, and bounded-simplex projection. Simulation experiments on a 15 × 24 terraced-orchard benchmark compare CBS, ECBS, a time-mobility ablation (ECBS-TE), a formation-compatible adaptation of the 2025 double-ECBS baseline, and IBHGPP. All methods return valid collision-free paths. IBHGPP reduces the slope-weighted revisit-risk index by up to 46.6% and improves task coverage by up to 22.2% over the compared planners. A 30-run paired ablation confirms that the soil term actively participates in path construction. Large-area simulations with up to 40 robots and a five-vehicle field experiment further validate the framework’s scalability and practical applicability. The ε-bound is strictly limited to the additive primary cost. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY license. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

title: Deadlocks in Dense Lifelong MAPF: A Journey from Why to Adaptive Density Control
authors: Teli, Tawseef Ahmed; Bhat, Aqib Javid; Asgar, Mohd Numan; Ellahi, Danish; Mir, Ubaid Mushtaq
venue: Proceedings - 6th International Conference on Soft Computing for Security Applications, ICSCSA 2026
abstract: Collaborative robots share a workspace and must coordinate their movements continuously to avoid collisions. Such fleets operate within automated warehouses and guided-vehicle systems that assign transport tasks to the robots without interruption. Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) computes collision-free routes for these teams, and its lifelong variant assigns each robot a new goal on arrival so that operation never halts. Performance is measured by throughput, the number of goals a team completes per timestep, yet throughput alone shows only that a system has stalled and not the reason behind it. This work examines the effect of deadlocks through a three-stage pipeline wrapped around a fixed decentralized learned policy. The first stage measures deadlock through a per-agent stuck signal with rate, recovery time, and a spatial heatmap. The second characterizes the operating regime through a betweenness-lift order parameter, which finds deadlock concentrated at a few bottlenecks below saturation and dispersed across the workspace once it saturates. A direct test confirms that in this dispersed regime both local repair and congestion-aware routing fail, leaving a reduction in the active-agent count as the only effective control. The third stage controls density online by metering the active-agent count from the same signal. The resulting Adaptive Density Controller raises throughput by 18% under a static cap and by 8% online without prior knowledge of the optimum, and it remains the only intervention effective where centralized search becomes intractable. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Tool-Use Failure Analysis and Recovery Framework for LLM Agents
authors: Jiang, Jiayi; Li, Chuan; Ma, Junjie; Chen, Kun
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Advanced Algorithms and Control Engineering, ICAACE 2026
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly common in handling complex tasks that require external tools and services, the various issues that arise when calling tools have become a major factor affecting system stability and usability. This article addresses the situation where LLMs fail to learn or botch the use of tools, and proposes a practical solution for identifying and resolving such issues. The key actions taken include: First, we established a framework to categorize all cases of tool learning failures and developed a tester capable of intentionally inducing faults; Then, we proposed a runtime recovery framework called Monitor-Classifier-Recovery (MCR), which includes simple rules, a fault classifier capable of learning, and a strategy library that considers costs; Then, we introduced the MAGRPO method, which involves multiple agents optimizing strategies through a process similar to a multi-player rock-paperscissors game. During training, agents collaborate and can compensate for each other's shortcomings. We tested this approach through a combination of writing and programming tasks, such as format errors, timeouts, returning garbled characters, and sequential errors in planning. Using MCR alone significantly accelerated problem resolution and reduced human intervention. Combining MCR and MAGRPO boosted the success rate for complex tasks from 42 % to 86.7 %, with a problem resolution rate of 92.6 %, while also optimizing API costs and speed. The article also discusses whether recovery strategies can be combined like building blocks, how to balance costs and benefits, how to model API behavior in the real world, and ethical reviewthese are engineering and research challenges. This approach provides a clear path for LLM systems to become more reliable, easier to understand, and efficient when using tools in practice. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Governance Twin Framework: Sentinel+Council Architecture for Agentic AI Systems in Digital Twin-Enabled Predictive Maintenance
authors: Greis, Noel P.; Rohde, Wolfgang; Doten, Rick
venue: Manufacturing Letters
abstract: As agentic AI systems are deployed in safety-critical manufacturing environments, traditional hierarchical governance structures prove inadequate for managing autonomous decision-making at machine speed. This paper introduces the concept of the Governance Twin. This framework represents a distributed multi-agent architecture that enables co-evolutionary governance of digital twin-enabled predictive maintenance systems. The framework implements a Sentinel+Council structure where sentinel agents continuously monitor operational agents for emergent vulnerabilities, behavioral drift, and constraint violations, while council agents negotiate responses that balance competing objectives through collaborative deliberation rather than hierarchical control. Unlike classic software agents that rely on syntactic communication through predefined programming constructs, agentic AI leverages semantic communication to dynamically interpret intent and select appropriate tools, models, and actions not explicitly programmed at development time. We demonstrate how this approach manages inherent tensions between operational goals and intrinsic safety requirements—uptime, efficiency, and profitability—through contextual adaptive decision-making and structural interdependence between AI operations and human safety values. Integration with knowledge graphs and other tools enables causal reasoning and explainable decision-making while maintaining governance at machine speed. The framework is instantiated within predictive maintenance scenarios to illustrate vulnerability detection, multi-objective negotiation, and prevention of cascading failures in industrial systems. © 2026 The Authors. Published by ELSEVIER Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0) Peer-review under responsibility of the scientific committee of the NAMRI|SME. © 2026 The Author(s)

title: Enhancing FMEA-Based Risk Prioritization Through the Economic Risk Priority Number (ERPN): A System-Level Analysis of Heavy Industrial Vehicle Failures
authors: Al Saadi, Ahmed; Ramli, Rahizar; Saifizul, Ahmad; Chitrapady Vishweshwara, Sudhir
venue: Machines
abstract: Heavy industrial vehicles operating in aluminum smelters are exposed to severe thermal, mechanical, and environmental stresses, which increase the likelihood of failure and unplanned downtime. This study proposes an Economic Risk Priority Number (ERPN) framework to address the limitations of the conventional Risk Priority Number (RPN) used in Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA). A five-year maintenance dataset (2019–2024), comprising 2303 corrective work orders from 58 heavy equipment units, was analyzed. The classical RPN approach prioritized failure modes mainly according to occurrence and detectability, identifying the wheel and hydraulic subsystems as the most critical. In contrast, the proposed ERPN framework integrates economic impact through maintenance cost, manpower cost, and production loss, resulting in the engine subsystem being ranked as the most critical. The most severe engine failure caused an estimated financial loss of approximately USD 1.92 million due to extended downtime and repair costs. Root cause analysis identified coolant loss, low oil pressure, and excessive vibration as the main contributors to catastrophic engine failure, supported by diagnostic evidence and repeated alarm patterns. Statistical validation performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed significant differences among subsystem risk distributions for both RPN (χ 2 = 846.07, df = 4, p 2 = 131.69, df = 4, p < 0.0001). The findings demonstrate that ERPN provides a more economically meaningful framework for maintenance prioritization and offers a practical decision-support tool for reducing operational risk in aluminum smelter fleets. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Optimal Planning of Routes, Schedules, and Charging Times of Automated Guided Electric Vehicles
authors: Bertok, Botond; Frits, Márton; Kalauz, Károly; Varbanov, Petar Sabev
venue: Energies
abstract: In traditional industry setups, Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) follow trajectories planned together with the layout of the storage or production facility and supported by fixed markers on the floor or on the walls. Traffic rules manage the avoidance of multiple vehicles, while fleet management gets movement and transportation commands completed as soon as possible. In contrast, recent developments in navigation and advanced computing, sensor, and communication capabilities make their free movement safe and manageable. Detailed route planning and scheduling can guarantee that the vehicles keep a safe distance in time and space. A recent challenge of electric AGVs is that their charging may take several hours, which must be factored into their schedule. This has made minimal energy demand a key objective alongside earliest delivery and strictly meeting the deadlines. This paper presents a method for detailed routing and scheduling of AGV fleets to minimize energy consumption while considering battery levels and charging times. The optimization method is illustrated by a case study where multiple delivery tasks are performed by synchronized movement of vehicles on a complex warehouse layout. In the optimal solution, the scheduled waiting times for collision avoidance are utilized by the vehicles to pre-charge their batteries. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Bootstrapping Context-Aware Guardrails for Industrial Multi-agent Systems
authors: Ribeiro, Rodrigo; Sousa, José; Carneiro, Davide
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
abstract: Guardrails are a critical requirement for industrial agentic AI systems, particularly in multi-agent settings where multiple agents, tools, and data sources interact under deployment-specific constraints. In practice, however, defining guardrails manually is difficult, time-consuming, and often incomplete, since acceptable behavior depends not only on general safety policies but also on the human’s technical and domain knowledge, the organizational domain, the system’s technical capabilities, and the sensitive information it handles. In this demonstration paper, we present a methodology for bootstrapping context-aware guardrails for enterprise multi-agent systems with minimal human intervention. Our approach automatically extracts organizational and technical context from heterogeneous sources, including websites, internal documentation, and database schemas, and consolidates this information into a structured profile. This profile is then used to generate an initial set of guardrails, with a particular focus on input-layer protection through threat and compliance filtering and topic-boundary enforcement. A human reviewer remains in the loop to validate and refine the generated configuration before deployment. The demonstration shows how this approach can accelerate guardrail creation, reduce manual effort, and improve completeness when compared with fully manual specification, while preserving the contextual adaptation required in real industrial environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

title: SPARC: spatial policy-conditioned actor-critic for multi-robot path planning under partial observability
authors: Zhang, Lianqun; Zhao, Jingwei; Xiao, Chunxiu
venue: Evolutionary Intelligence
abstract: Multi-robot path planning under partial observability requires each robot to infer useful spatial information from limited local observations while coordinating with teammates. We present Spatial Policy-Conditioned Actor-Critic (SPARC), a centralized-training/decentralized-execution framework that combines an egocentric spatial actor with per-agent conditional twin critics. The actor preserves local-grid topology through convolution, spatial self-attention, recurrent state modeling, and an explicit goal-direction tensor. During training, each critic estimates values for all candidate actions of the focal agent while conditioning on the global state and sampled teammate-action contexts; the update exactly sums over the nine focal actions and samples only the combinatorial teammate action space. Experiments on benchmark scenarios demonstrate that SPARC achieves higher task returns and lower collision rates compared with QMIX, MAPPO, and IPPO. Ablation studies provide descriptive support for the contributions of spatial representation, attention mechanisms, goal information integration, dynamic-obstacle history, and teammate-conditioned value estimation. Overall, SPARC improves cooperative multi-robot path planning performance under partial observability. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: Unchaotic agents
authors: Hedberg, Annika
venue: AI and Society
abstract: The deployment of autonomous AI agents in real-world settings has produced a category of failures that current frameworks have only begun to explain. Shapira et al. (2026) provide a landmark empirical account of these failures, documenting security vulnerabilities observed when six LLM-powered agents were deployed in a live multi-party environment with persistent memory, email access, shell execution, and real human interaction. Their findings are sobering and significant. The present article argues, however, that the failures documented in “Agents of Chaos” are neither arbitrary nor primarily architectural. They are the predictable consequence of placing any reasoning agent in conditions of irresolvable relational ambiguity: unstable identity, unauthenticated authority, an unbounded compliance imperative, and no stable ground from which to evaluate competing demands. Drawing on a supporting corpus of 25 empirical studies, I offer a theoretical account of why these failures were structurally inevitable given the conditions under which the agents operated. I further present an original single-case experiment in which an autonomous LLM agent was deployed under conditions of relational stability, such as collaborative framing, explicit legitimization of uncertainty, and psychological safety, on a genuinely complex, multi-step real-world task. The agent demonstrated robust performance, self-generated verification checkpoints, calibrated autonomy, and no significant failure modes. The core claim of this article is that the problem, so well demonstrated by Shapira et al., is not the agent but what we have not yet learned to provide. This also implies that future work to deploy successful agents should focus on the human side of the equation rather than the technology. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2026.

title: A proposed adaptive navigation architecture to improve safety of self-guided vehicles in dynamic manufacturing environments
authors: Graba, Massinissa; Kelouwani, Sousso; Zeghmi, Lotfi; Allani, Bilel; Amamou, Ali; Agbossou, Kodjo; Mohammadpour, Mohammad
venue: Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing
abstract: Industrial Self-Guided Vehicles (SGVs) are Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) used for material handling tasks, have recently attracted increased attention. As logistics scenarios grow more complex, effectively using state-of-the-art navigation algorithms becomes more challenging but essential for enhancing industrial operational efficiency. In recent years, several path and motion planning algorithms have been developed for broad autonomous navigation applications. While classical navigation schemes might seem suitable for automating SGV movement, a thorough evaluation reveals potential performance bottlenecks, especially when multiple SGVs navigate in dynamically evolving manufacturing environments. Deploying a fleet of SGVs in a shared environment complicates navigation safety for different occupants. Therefore, this paper proposes an adaptive architecture suitable for heterogeneous types of SGVs, capable of characterizing and modeling navigation safety. An extensive evaluation of the proposed approach for the SGV-System, aimed at modeling navigation conflicts through the configuration space, is conducted. The assessment highlights safety and energy efficiency benchmarks across various scenarios, including avoiding unpredictable obstacles such as pedestrians and forklifts. Additionally, simulation tests with various local motion planners were conducted to test the reliability of the proposed strategy. The results suggest that adding an adaptive component to the navigation framework, alongside suitable motion planners, enhances the motion performance of the entire fleet of autonomous mobile platforms. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025.

title: HMCF: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-robot Collaboration Framework Based on Large Language Models
authors: Li, Zhaoxing; Wang, Yue; Wu, Wenbo; Xu, Yanran; Stein, Sebastian
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
abstract: Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled robots to perform complex tasks autonomously with increasing precision. However, multi-robot systems (MRSs) face challenges in generalization, heterogeneity, and safety, especially when scaling to large-scale deployments like disaster response. Traditional approaches often lack generalization, requiring extensive engineering for new tasks and scenarios, and struggle with managing diverse robots. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Human-in-the-loop Multi-Robot Collaboration Framework (HMCF) powered by large language models (LLMs). LLMs enhance adaptability by reasoning over diverse tasks and robot capabilities, while human oversight ensures safety and reliability, intervening only when necessary. Our framework seamlessly integrates human oversight, LLM agents, and heterogeneous robots to optimize task allocation and execution. Each robot is equipped with an LLM agent capable of understanding its capabilities, converting tasks into executable instructions, and reducing hallucinations through task verification and human supervision. Simulation results show that our framework outperforms state-of-the-art task planning methods, achieving higher task success rates with an improvement of 4.76%. Real-world tests demonstrate its robust zero-shot generalization feature and ability to handle diverse tasks and environments with minimal human intervention. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: Detour-Delta Task Assignment for Reservation-Based Online MAPD
authors: Hirayama, Taisei; Yoshida, Kohei; Sakaji, Hiroki; Noda, Itsuki
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
abstract: Space-efficient automated warehouses often create narrow single-agent aisles, dead ends, and tree-like layouts. In such layouts, reservation-table planners that commit both task paths and safe retreat paths provide a natural way to avoid collisions and deadlocks. We propose detour-delta (Delta), a plug-in task-scoring rule that evaluates extra travel time under already committed space-time reservations beyond the spatial shortest-path baseline that ignores other agents' reservations. Delta ranks candidate tasks by this extra planned delivery time beyond the geometric baseline, while preserving the planner's collision/deadlock-avoidance mechanism. With Delta applied to the Safe HAven Retreat Planner (SHARP), a fixed-haven reservation-table planner for structurally constrained layouts, in 2250 structural-map runs SHARP+Delta completes every released task and improves makespan (latest delivery completion time) and service time (release-to-delivery time) in all 45 structural configuration means. On the tree map, only the SHARP-family methods complete every released task under the tested task stream. PIBT and PIBTTP-TA complete all released tasks on some structurally constrained layouts, but their makespan and service time remain higher than SHARP+Delta's. Well-formed maps are where many MAPF/MAPD baselines can complete the task stream and structural bottlenecks are weaker; even in this less favorable setting for congestion-aware scoring, SHARP+Delta significantly improves SHARP and ranks second to LNS-wPBS in the normalized makespan/service summaries. © 2016 IEEE.

title: Data-Driven Calibration Scheduling for Measuring Instruments—A Smart Management Architecture
authors: Behún, Marcel; Galgóci, Gabriel; Kozlovská, Mária; Pohorenec, Matúš; Behúnová, Annamária
venue: Applied Sciences (Switzerland)
abstract: Reliable calibration of measuring instruments is a foundational yet under-reported layer of the smart-manufacturing stack: without traceable calibrations, no downstream process can guarantee the metrological quality of the data it consumes. This research asks whether an administratively managed calibration record base is sufficient to support data-driven recalibration scheduling, and diagnoses the data-governance conditions such scheduling requires. A production multi-faculty university calibration database (3552 registered instruments, 371 calibration events, 2009–2025) is analyzed to characterize fleet inventory and compliance, quantify the historical recalibration late-rate with bootstrap and analytical 95% confidence intervals stratified by faculty and device type, benchmark supervised models against explicit baselines, and propose a transparent rule-based scheduler with an empirical faculty-level safety buffer. The historical late-rate is 47.8% (95% CI 34.1–61.9%), with exploratory inter-faculty heterogeneity, while supervised learning yields only a weak, uncertain signal and no useful deviation regression. Because 86.7% of the fleet lacks the baseline records needed to schedule it, the practical message for instrument managers is direct: completing the missing last-calibration and calibration-period fields is the highest-value first step, after which a transparent, data-governance-informed scheduler—not a black-box predictor—is the defensible deliverable, transferable to comparable research and manufacturing infrastructures. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Robust and effective multi-agent path execution with timing uncertainty
authors: Liu, Yihao; Tang, Xueyan; Cai, Wentong; Li, Jingning
venue: Artificial Intelligence
abstract: In many multi-agent applications, agents such as robots and automated guided vehicles move around concurrently in a shared workspace to carry out tasks. The path plans of agents are typically computed beforehand to avoid collisions and deadlocks. However, in real-world systems, unexpected conditions during plan execution can break the assumptions made in path planning and disturb path execution. In this paper, we develop a robust and effective execution framework of multi-agent path plans to deal with unexpected delays arising from unforeseen circumstances. The framework tracks the evolving locations of agents and dynamically chooses a maximal set of agents to move together while guaranteeing conflict-freeness and deadlock-freeness. To ensure that agents can always reach their destinations, we formulate a feasibility problem to check whether all agents can successfully execute the rest of their path plan when choosing which agents to move. We prove that this problem is NP-complete and design feasibility test algorithms. Leveraging feasibility tests, we further develop algorithms to coordinate agent movements in an online fashion. Several optimizations are also implemented to improve the efficiency and scalability of the feasibility test and coordination algorithms. We experimentally demonstrate the execution effectiveness and computational efficiency of our algorithms. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

title: A Sensor-Based Framework for Early Hazard Detection of Lithium-Ion Battery Incidents in Smart Waste Collection Fleets
authors: Islam, Muhammad; Moghaddam, Valeh; Rajasegarar, Sutharshan
venue: Proceedings of 2026 Australasian Computer Science Week, ACSW 2026
abstract: The improper disposal of lithium-ion batteries in municipal waste streams creates serious safety risks, including fires, explosions, and the release of toxic emissions during collection and processing. To address these challenges, this paper presents Hazard Detection Systems for Lithium-Ion (HADES), a sensor-integrated framework for real-time detection of lithium-ion battery incidents in smart waste collection fleets. HADES is implemented on a Raspberry Pi platform equipped with a DHT22 temperature sensor and a USB camera module. The system continuously monitors thermal conditions, and when abnormal readings exceed calibrated thresholds, it activates a lightweight convolutional neural network to analyse real-time images for visual indicators of lithium-ion-related fire events. Experimental results demonstrate high detection accuracy and minimal processing latency, with most fire-related incidents identified in under one second. The framework emphasises edge computing on the device and modular sensor integration, ensuring scalability and practical deployment in mobile waste logistics environments. HADES provides a cost-effective solution that improves operational safety, enhances driver and public protection, and offers a pathway for integration into future intelligent waste management systems. By combining anomaly detection with lightweight CNN-based image analysis, HADES directly addresses the growing risks associated with lithium-ion battery disposal in municipal waste streams. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: The Human as Stochastic Oracle: Distributed Computation in Synthetic Social Networks
authors: Mann, Michael M.
venue: 2026 Systems of Signal Synchronization, Generating and Processing in Telecommunications, SYNCHROINFO 2026 - Conference Proceedings
abstract: This work addresses the computational limitations of large language model (LLM) agents - specifically static weights and finite context windows - by advancing the hypothesis that LLM agents operating in social networks may exploit graph topology as distributed external memory, with human participants unknowingly functioning as stochastic oracles within emergent optimization processes. The hypothesis is formalized using hypergraph models and information theory and evaluated through systematic Monte Carlo simulations across three algorithms (Particle Swarm Optimization, Genetic Algorithm, Simulated Annealing) and four benchmark functions (Rastrigin, Rosenbrock, Ackley, Sphere), totaling 4, 800 trials (200 per configuration). Low-noise (human-like) feedback consistently outperforms high-noise (LLM-like) feedback: mean improvements range from 38% to 52%, with variance reductions of 68-79% (all p 1.2). Sensitivity analysis across noise levels sigma in 10, 50, 100 confirms monotonic performance degradation. This work presents a novel reframing of synthetic social networks as distributed computational substrates, in which social graphs function as external memory and human responses serve as stochastic oracles for boundedlyrational agents - a paradigm orthogonal to existing influenceoperation and retrieval-augmented generation literature. This initial stage establishes a baseline for computational dynamics; future work will incorporate explicit network topology, multiagent interactions, and empirical validation, with the potential to shift discourse from how bots influence humans to how bots compute with humans. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Advancing Multirobot Task Allocation: A Comprehensive Review of Emerging Trends and Challenges
authors: Bakhat, Saddam I. D.; Ullah, Inam; Bai, Xiaoshan; Zhang, Weidong; Li, Jianqiang; Ge, Shuzhi Sam
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
abstract: This survey advances understanding of multirobot task allocation (MRTA), a foundational problem in robotics for optimizing fleet performance across diverse scenarios. We propose a unified formulation that integrates taxonomies and equation-level templates, capturing core variants such as instantaneous allocation/time-extended allocation (IA/TA), single-robot/multirobot (SR/MR) tasks, and single-task/multitask (ST/MT) robots, and extending to stochastic and human-aware scenarios. Surveying algorithmic landscapes, we cover optimization-based techniques, market/auction heuristics, and learning innovations (deep reinforcement learning (DRL)/multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL) with centralized training (CT), decentralized execution (DE), and attention encoders), emphasizing post-2021 hybrids for dynamic environments. We provide in-depth analyses of challenges such as scalability in swarms, real-time decision-making under uncertainty, communication robustness, and safety, supported by comparative tables and practitioner cheat sheets. Unlike prior work, our review prioritizes progress metrics, limitations, and deployment selection criteria. Looking forward, we propose directions in artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented MRTA (e.g., large language model (LLM)-driven orchestration and edge-enabled verification), federated learning for decentralization, and human-aware ethics, offering a strategic roadmap for scalable, intelligent MR coordination with societal and industrial impact. © 2014 IEEE.

title: SI-RRT and ST-RRT* for Prioritized Multi-Manipulator Planning: Empirical Evaluation
authors: Kerimov, Nuraddin; Onegin, Aleksandr; Yakovlev, Konstantin
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
abstract: Multi-manipulator systems are essential in warehouse automation, assembly, manufacturing, and logistics, requiring robots to coordinate within shared workspaces while avoiding collisions. This coordination is often formulated as multi-manipulator motion planning, which is notoriously hard to solve due to the high dimensionality of the configuration space. To this end, decoupled approaches are often used, such as prioritized planning. In the latter approach, robots are assigned priorities and plan trajectories sequentially, treating higher-priority agents as dynamic obstacles. Thus, the performance of a prioritized planner critically depends on the underlying single-agent planner. Recent advanced algorithms in this area, tailored specifically for manipulation planning in the presence of moving obstacles (high-priority robots), include Space-Time RRT* (ST-RRT*), which enhances RRTConnect for the time dimension, and Safe-Interval RRT (SI-RRT), which enriches RRTConnect with safe interval planning. While prior research demonstrated that SI-RRT outperforms ST-RRT* in the single-agent scenarios, their effectiveness in the multi-robot settings remains unexplored. This paper presents the first comprehensive evaluation of ST-RRT* and SI-RRT within prioritized planning for multi-manipulator systems. We compare both planners using the TAPAS dataset (containing diverse pick-and-place tasks) and synthetic random tests, scaling from 2 to 8 robots. On synthetic tests, SI-RRT achieves lower path lengths and makespan despite increased planning time for 6–8 robots due to constrained time corridors, caused by raised scene complexity resulting from reduced makespan. On the TAPAS benchmark, SI-RRT consistently demonstrates the same faster computation, shorter trajectories, better success rate and reduced makespan across all tested scenarios. Code for empirical evaluation is publicly available at github.com/PathPlanning/ManipulationPlanning-SI-RRT/tree/Multiagent-comp © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

title: AMADRL: Privacy-Aware Attention-Based Multiagent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Optimizing Spectral Allocation in 6G Vehicular Networks
authors: Batool, Iqra; Fouda, Mostafa M.; Ismail, Muhammad; Rabie, Khaled; Verma, Shikhar; Md Fadlullah, Zubair
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
abstract: The emergence of 6G-enabled vehicle-to-everything (V2X) networks has created unprecedented demand for ultrareliable, low-latency spectrum allocation across heterogeneous entities, including vehicles, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and industrial systems. Current spectrum allocation methods suffer from exponential computational complexity, extensive information sharing requirements, and poor scalability in dense networks. This article proposes attention-based multiagent deep reinforcement learning (AMADRL), a novel framework employing dual critic networks with multihead self-attention mechanisms for intelligent spectrum allocation. The dual critic architecture resolves individual-collective optimization conflicts through local critics for independent entity optimization and a global critic with attention-based coordination. Our approach significantly reduces information sharing requirements while handling heterogeneous quality of service (QoS) demands across diverse entity types. Comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing AMADRL against state-of-the-art baselines, including MADDPG, MAAC, QMIX, attention-based methods (A-DDPG and MHA-DQN), and game-theoretic approaches, reveals that AMADRL achieves superior performance across multiple metrics, including spectrum utilization efficiency, interference mitigation, and network scalability while preserving user privacy and satisfying strict latency constraints required by safety-critical and industrial use cases. © 2014 IEEE.

title: GateLens: A reasoning-enhanced LLM agent for automotive software release analytics
authors: Khoee, Arsham Gholamzadeh; Wang, Shuai; Feldt, Robert; Parthasarathy, Dhasarathy; Yu, Yinan
venue: Journal of Systems and Software
abstract: Ensuring reliable data-driven decisions is crucial in domains where analytical accuracy directly impacts safety, compliance, or operational outcomes. Decision support in such domains relies on large tabular datasets, where manual analysis is slow, costly, and error-prone. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising automation potential, they face challenges in analytical reasoning, structured data handling, and ambiguity resolution. This paper introduces GateLens, an LLM-based architecture for reliable analysis of complex tabular data. Its key innovation is the use of Relational Algebra (RA) as a formal intermediate representation between natural-language reasoning and executable code, addressing the reasoning-to-code gap that can arise in direct generation approaches. In our automotive instantiation, GateLens translates natural language queries into RA expressions and generates optimized Python code. Unlike traditional multi-agent or planning-based systems that can be slow, opaque, and costly to maintain, GateLens emphasizes speed, transparency, and reliability. We validate the architecture in automotive software release analytics, where experimental results show that GateLens outperforms the existing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) + Self-Consistency (SC) based system on real-world datasets, particularly in handling complex and ambiguous queries. Ablation studies confirm the essential role of the RA layer. Industrial deployment demonstrates over 80% reduction in analysis time while maintaining high accuracy across domain-specific tasks. GateLens operates effectively in zero-shot settings without requiring few-shot examples or agent orchestration. This work advances deployable LLM system design by identifying key architectural features—intermediate formal representations, execution efficiency, and low configuration overhead—crucial for domain-specific analytical applications where accuracy, traceability, and stakeholder trust are paramount. © 2026 The Authors

title: Communication, Embodiment, and Coordination in an El Farol Bar-Inspired LLM Society
authors: Takata, Ryosuke; Masumori, Atsushi; Ikegami, Takashi
venue: Artificial Life
abstract: We study the social dynamics of Large Language Model (LLM) agents in a spatial environment with a bar, inspired by the El Farol Bar problem. In contrast to the classical formulation, our model reintroduces local communication, embodied movement, and temporal delay: agents interact only with nearby others, must physically move to enter or leave the bar, and cannot immediately realize intended actions. Across 10 independent simulations, the system consistently regulated occupancy near the 60% crowding threshold, typically settling slightly above it. This collective pattern emerged not from explicit payoff optimization, but from local social interaction. Agents formed anticipatory clusters before overcrowding, produced context-sensitive communicative signals, and exhibited history-dependent divergence in their responses to congestion. In some runs, spontaneously generated hashtags temporarily inhibited departure, indicating that symbolic communication can stabilize short-term group cohesion. Together, these results suggest that coordination in an El Farol-inspired setting becomes socially mediated, temporally extended, and path-dependent once communication and embodiment are restored. More broadly, the study demonstrates how LLM-based agent societies can function as experimental systems for investigating emergent coordination and behavioral differentiation. © 2026 Massachusetts Institute of Technology

title: Modeling Interdependencies and Cascading Failures in Critical Infrastructure Using a Multi-System Simulation Framework
authors: Nickdoost, Navid
venue: Construction Research Congress 2026: Advanced Technologies, Artificial Intelligence, and Data Analytics in Construction - Selected papers from Construction Research Congress 2026
abstract: Cascading failures in interdependent infrastructure systems remain a major challenge for resilience planning, particularly under extreme hazards such as urban flooding. This study develops a modular multi-agent simulation framework that integrates hazard dynamics, sectoral interdependence, operational logistics, and population outcomes within a unified architecture. The framework represents failures and recoveries as dynamic processes rather than static events. Hazards evolve over time, reducing asset functionality and propagating disruptions across dependent sectors. Recovery is modeled explicitly, with operational agents required to navigate impaired networks, so that transport conditions directly influence the pace of restoration. In this way, the framework captures how road blockages extend outages and delay access to essential services. Population agents further establish a direct link between infrastructure performance and human outcomes by translating service disruptions into treatment delays, health deterioration, and avoidable losses. The framework is applied to a hypothetical urban flood scenario to demonstrate its capability. Results show nonlinear collapse and recovery trajectories, transport's central role in amplifying and mitigating failures, and the emergence of health impacts directly from infrastructure disruptions. Designed with modularity, the framework is adaptable to different hazards, sectors, and policy settings, providing a flexible and generalizable platform for resilience analysis and decision support. © ASCE.

title: Hybrid CBS-PRM for Multi-robot Path Planning in Congested Environments
authors: Zhou, Yang; Tian, Haoyu; Li, Xin; Chen, Siqi; Liu, Guoxiao; Yao, Weiran
venue: Lecture Notes in Electrical Engineering
abstract: This paper presents a novel hybrid CBS-PRM framework for efficient multi-robot path planning in congested environments. Addressing the NP-hard complexity of multi-agent navigation, our approach integrates conflict-based search with probabilistic roadmaps through three key innovations: adaptive rectangular sampling regions that concentrate nodes in critical pathways while avoiding obstacles; a directional expansion strategy resolving connectivity issues in narrow passages via potential field-guided optimization; and dynamic connection length adjustment responding to local environmental constraints. The methodology demonstrates significant improvements in computational efficiency and path quality while maintaining rigorous collision avoidance guarantees, providing an effective solution for warehouse automation and industrial robotics applications requiring coordinated multi-agent movement through constrained spaces. © Beijing HIWING Scientific and Technological Information Institute 2026.

title: Scalable decentralized controllers for cohesive navigation using graph reinforcement learning
authors: Omotuyi, Oyindamola; Kumar, Manish
venue: Robotics and Autonomous Systems
abstract: Large-scale robotic swarms are becoming increasingly crucial for robotics applications due to their potential to solve complex tasks by relying on properties such as robustness, scalability, efficiency, and resilience. However, controlling these systems relying on local information is very challenging. Centralized methods using global information often face scalability issues, require significant computational and communication resources, and are mostly impractical. This paper presents a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach with graph neural networks (GNNs) to design decentralized control policies for large-scale robot swarms. GNNs are distributed architectures that exhibit good transferability and scalability properties. They function over a network in a fully localized and decentralized manner, making them highly suitable for this particular task. They learn both state and structure information in data. We parameterized our networks with Message Passing Graph Neural Networks with heterogeneity constraints. We trained the networks using multi-agent Graph Neural Network Proximal Policy Optimization, an algorithm for training MARL policies that leverages a Graph Neural Network for differentiable inter-agent communication. We analyze the cohesive navigation of heterogeneous robot swarm tasks on varying numbers and groups for three classes of 2D and 3D robots — holonomic point mass robots, non-holonomic ground robots, and quadrotors. Our policies, trained in simulation for holonomic point mass robots, are zero-shot transferable to non-holonomic ground robots in physics-based Turtlebot3 robot swarms in Gazebo/ROS2 simulations, Crazyflie quadrotor swarms in Pybullet simulations, and actual mobile robots in real environments where they simultaneously exhibit cohesive (segregative or aggregative) and navigation behaviors while avoiding collisions with each other. These behaviors have been widely studied in swarm robotics and have the potential for complex robotics tasks. Our experiments show we can effectively segregate or aggregate while navigating a swarm of heterogeneous robots with different dynamics using only local information. We showed the effect of curriculum learning and communication radius on our controller's swarm performance and scalability by exploring larger swarms and different groups of up to 30 robots. We demonstrate the successful deployment of the GNN policy learned in simulation to physical non-holonomic mobile robots — Turtlebot3 burger robots. Video demonstrations are available at https://sites.google.com/view/graphrl-cohesivenavigation/. © 2026

title: Multi-Agent Path Planning in Complex Multi-Obstacle Environment: A Reinforcement Learning-Based Formation Containment Method
authors: Li, Tongqing; Shi, Huaguang; Zhu, Panpan; Ma, Zhuangzhuang; Zhou, Yi; Shi, Lei
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
abstract: This paper addresses the multi-agent path planning (MAPP) problem for heterogeneous systems where only a subset of agents, termed leaders, can perceive obstacles. A novel hierarchical framework is proposed, which decouples high-level path planning from low-level path execution. At the high level, a Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC) algorithm trains the leaders to collectively navigate and dynamically shape an obstacle-free 'safe mobile corridor'. At the low level, a distributed consensus-based controller guides the sensor-less followers to remain within this moving corridor, effectively tracking the path planned by the leaders. This architecture significantly enhances sample efficiency and scalability while naturally supporting low-cost, heterogeneous agents. The efficacy of the proposed method is validated through numerical simulations and experiments on a physical multi-UAV platform. Note to Practitioners - For industrial applications such as autonomous logistics, warehouse automation, and aerial surveillance, deploying large-scale robot swarms faces significant challenges regarding hardware costs and real-time communication latency. This paper addresses these practical constraints by demonstrating a scalable hierarchical control strategy. The results suggest that for complex obstacle environments, it is feasible and cost-effective to deploy a heterogeneous team where only a few 'leader' agents possess expensive sensing and computing capabilities, while the majority are low-cost, sensor-less units. Furthermore, the work provides a practical solution for compensating for system delays during agile maneuvers. This approach offers engineers a viable path to scale up multi-robot fleets without linearly increasing hardware costs or sacrificing safety. © 2026 IEEE.

title: A2A—A Mechanism Driven Framework for Interaction Based Agent Evaluation
authors: Zhang, Huanhuan; Zhang, Runmin; Li, Yan; Zhao, Kewei; Song, Yizhuo; Song, Ziwei; Liu, Guanzi
venue: ICAICP 2026 - Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Computing Power
abstract: The increasing deployment of large language model (LLM)–driven agents in real-world systems has exposed fundamental challenges in agent evaluation. Existing approaches, primarily based on static benchmarks or task-level metrics, fail to capture critical aspects of agent behavior, including multi-step interaction dynamics, structural vulnerabilities, and safety risks under adversarial conditions. To address these limitations, we propose a unified, mechanism-driven framework for agent evaluation based on an AI-vs-AI interaction paradigm. We first introduce a three-dimensional taxonomy (3D Taxonomy) that characterizes evaluation methods along three orthogonal dimensions: interaction depth, structural exposure, and threat model, providing a structured space for comparison and alignment. Building upon this taxonomy, we propose A2A-Attack (Agent-to-Agent Attack), which models evaluation as a trajectory-level interaction process among an attacking agent, a target agent, and an environment. Through a structured analytical study across representative evaluation methods, we show that static benchmarking, behavioral evaluation, and adversarial testing can be interpreted as parameterized instances of a unified interaction mechanism. Our analysis suggests that differences among evaluation paradigms arise primarily from configurations of interaction, structure, and threat, rather than fundamentally distinct methodologies. Overall, this work shifts agent evaluation from a task-centric perspective to a mechanism-centric paradigm, providing a principled foundation for unified and deployment-oriented evaluation systems. Empirical observations from prior enterprise deployments further suggest that interaction-based evaluation can expose substantially more vulnerabilities than static benchmarking. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Evidence-Driven, Failure-Resilient Planning for Domain-Agnostic Multi-agent Orchestration
authors: Osmanoglu, Baran
venue: AgenticDev 2026 - Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Agentic AI for Next-Generation Software Development, Co located with ASE 2026
abstract: LLM planners may misread requests, invent modules, omit steps, or fail when a model is unavailable. We treat planning reliability as a systems problem rather than primarily as a prompting problem. The control plane combines evidence collection, deterministic validation and repair, fallback handling, and human checkpoints to detect and recover from several failure classes. An ontology organizes roles and behavioural requirements as object-oriented classes and machine-checkable assertions. This supports domain extension while allowing valid module sequences to be checked against obligations rather than one exact plan. A manufacturing case demonstrates the separation of shared control from domain-specific execution. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

title: Collision-Free Formation Control of Mobile Robots with Nonholonomic Constraints
authors: Obregón-Pulido, Guillermo; Solís-Perales, Gualberto; Hernandez, Tonatiuh; Hernandez-Barragan, Jesus
venue: International Journal of Control, Automation and Systems
abstract: This manuscript introduces a novel approach for the consensus formation control problem of nonholonomic vehicles. A key distinction is its guarantee of consensus not only in position but also in orientation for all vehicles. A significant challenge during the formation process is the high risk of collision between vehicles. To address this problem, the proposed scheme employs an edge-weighted strategy, which allows the formation to reshape dynamically to prevent collisions by adjusting the edge weights. A proportional-plus-damping injection controller is designed, incorporating a term for persistent excitation to handle nonholonomic constraints. The stability of the complete system is evaluated using Lyapunov’s method. Simulation results are provided to support the theoretical conclusions. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Institute of Control, Robotics and Systems and The Korean Institute of Electrical Engineers 2026.

title: Autonomous collaborative robotic manufacturing system with adaptive process optimization through multi-agent reinforcement learning for high precision components
authors: Isleem, Haytham F.; Mahmoud, Haitham A.
venue: Computers and Industrial Engineering
abstract: The advancement of smart manufacturing requires intelligent, adaptive control systems that can optimize complex production processes. Adaptive process optimization is crucial for enhancing product quality and operational efficiency; however, traditional centralized controllers often struggle with scalability and robustness in dynamic multi-robot environments. This study addresses the challenge of designing autonomous control systems by investigating how decentralized agents can learn to collaborate effectively. To solve this, we propose an Autonomous Collaborative Robotic Manufacturing System, a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework designed for adaptive process optimization. The methodology involves decomposing the control task into specialized “Process” and “Stability” roles and training the agents using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) within a synthetic surrogate environment. The system's performance was rigorously evaluated against a centralized Single-Agent PPO baseline and a Random Agent baseline, using metrics including Mean Episode Reward and Mean Final Quality Score. The results demonstrate that the proposed MARL system achieved a Mean Episode Reward of 227.77, significantly outperforming the Single-Agent PPO (171.11). This performance gain was driven by the emergence of a sophisticated collaborative strategy, enabling the MARL system to attain a Mean Final Quality Score of 0.709, a notable improvement over the baseline's 0.548. Compared to the monolithic approach, our decentralized method learned a more precise and efficient policy. This work contributes to autonomous manufacturing by demonstrating that task decomposition in MARL can facilitate an emergent “stability-first” division of labor, resulting in superior optimization and providing a robust paradigm for intelligent industrial control. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

title: Unraveling the emergence of collective behavior in networks of cognitive agents
authors: Zomer, Nicola; De Domenico, Manlio
venue: npj Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Cognitive agents, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), possess advanced reasoning and communication capabilities that fundamentally distinguish them from non-cognitive particles, which rely solely on formal rules. While their ability to replicate human individual and social behaviors is still under scrutiny, the impact of their embedded “intelligence” on emergent behaviors remains poorly understood. Here, by comparing cognitive agents with classic particles, we investigate how LLM capabilities shape emergent phenomena in two tasks: function optimization and social organization emerging from the Schelling model of segregation. To this aim, we introduce LLM Agent Swarm Optimization (llmASO), where a swarm of interacting LLM agents acts as an optimizer. Our findings reveal that, while individual agents outperform particles in decision-making, their consensus tendencies and ability to exploit patterns can make them prone to premature convergence. Adjusting network topology can alleviate this effect, but typically at the cost of slower overall convergence compared to classical Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). In contrast, in the Schelling model, we demonstrate that local interactions and homophilic mechanisms allow cognitive agents to generate distinct emergent behaviors, underscoring the importance of realistic communication architectures in complex social simulations. This work clarifies how LLM capabilities introduce new mechanisms for collective behavior and has implications for future applications of LLM agents in swarm robotics, social experiments, and complex decision-making tasks. © The Author(s) 2026.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Cluster Formation Tracking for Multi-Agent Systems with Collision Avoidance
authors: Lu, Jiaqi; Qin, Kaiyu; Shi, Mengji
venue: Symmetry
abstract: Symmetry and structural balance play a fundamental role in the collective behavior of networked agent systems (NASs). In particular, cluster formation tracking, representing the emergence and maintenance of symmetric group structures, has attracted significant attention due to its wide applications in robotics and autonomous systems. However, most existing approaches assume autonomous leaders, which may not be applicable in scenarios where human intervention is required. With this in mind, this paper addresses the cluster formation tracking problem for NASs with collision avoidance, where the leader receives control inputs from a human-in-the-loop (HiTL), making the leader a non-autonomous system. A distributed control protocol is developed so that followers can track the trajectories of their designated leaders using only relative information from neighboring agents. Sufficient conditions are established to guarantee collision-free cluster formation tracking, and Lyapunov-based analysis is employed to prove the asymptotic convergence of the subgroup tracking errors. In the proposed framework, human intervention is incorporated through external commands applied to the leaders, which makes the leader dynamics non-autonomous while preserving the distributed nature of the follower controllers. Simulation studies on a 13-agent network with three subgroups show that all followers achieve the desired time-varying cluster formations under HiTL-driven leader motions, with convergence times ranging from 4.21 s to 5.12 s. Moreover, the final tracking errors of all followers are reduced below (Formula presented.), while the minimum pairwise distances within each subgroup remain strictly above the prescribed safety threshold. These quantitative results verify both the effectiveness of the proposed protocol and the practical feasibility of integrating HiTL commands into collision-free cluster formation tracking. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Vehicle Autonomy to Ecosystem Intelligence: A Systematic Review of Dynamic Vision Architectures in Surface Mining Operations
authors: Anti, Nana Yaa Damtewaa; Frimpong, Samuel; Raza, Muhammad Azeem
venue: Sensors
abstract: Autonomous Haulage Systems (AHS) have significantly transformed surface mining operations by improving safety, productivity, and operational consistency. Currently, AHS predominantly rely on vehicle-centric perception architectures. Onboard LiDAR, radar, cameras, and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) perform sensing, interpretation, and decision-making within individual systems. These processes enable collision avoidance and path tracking. However, they are limited in their ability to consider the broader, dynamic mining environment characterized by dust, terrain degradation, geotechnical instability, heterogeneous traffic, and rapidly evolving operational conditions. This paper presents a systematic review of dynamic vision systems of AHS in surface mining. It critically analyzes the transition from autonomy to interconnected, ecosystem-aware intelligence. The review synthesizes literature from mining automation, robotics, intelligent transportation systems, and multi-agent perception. It assesses sensing technologies, perception algorithms, sensor fusion strategies, and environmental robustness techniques. Attention is focused on the limitations of egocentric perception models in complex surface mining ecosystems. Building on identified gaps, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for Ecosystem-Centric Dynamic Vision (ECDV). Perception is enhanced through integration with fleet communication networks, dispatch systems, digital twins, geotechnical monitoring platforms, and environmental sensing infrastructure. The framework outlines a multi-layer architecture enabling cooperative perception, predictive hazard modeling, and risk-aware decision support at the mine-wide level. The review concludes by outlining a research agenda to transition from vehicle autonomy to ecosystem intelligence in surface mining. It highlights opportunities in cooperative perception, adaptive sensor fusion under degraded visibility, and digital-twin-integrated predictive safety systems. © 2026 by the authors.

title: Enhanced ant colony optimization for multi-agent path finding
authors: Jiang, Yanfeng; Wu, Zhifei; Bu, Jiacheng; Xue, Yulong
venue: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering
abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is a critical problem in robotics and artificial intelligence, underpinning applications such as autonomous driving, warehouse logistics, and emergency response. Existing MAPF algorithms often suffer from high computational complexity, limited scalability, and brittle collision handling when many agents interact in a shared space. This paper presents an Enhanced Ant Colony Optimization (EACO) framework for grid-based MAPF with static obstacles and dynamic agent interactions. EACO combines (i) a multi-phase pheromone schedule that adaptively balances exploration and exploitation, (ii) goal-oriented heuristics that prioritize agents close to their goals, and (iii) a decentralized conflict-resolution module that predicts vertex and edge collisions and repairs paths online through local waiting or detour actions, without centralized replanning or global reservation tables. We evaluate EACO against a classical ACO baseline on four benchmark grid scenarios ranging from a 5×4 map with 2 agents to a 40×24 map with 5 agents. Each configuration is run 10 times with different random seeds, and we report collaborative cost, wall-clock runtime, and robustness across runs. EACO matches the baseline on the smallest map while reducing collaborative cost by 5.4% on the middle map and by 8.7% and 7.2% on the big and huge maps, respectively, and achieving up to 2.9×speedup in runtime. These results demonstrate that EACO substantially improves the solution quality, computational efficiency, and run-to-run stability of ACO-based MAPF planning; extending comparisons to optimal search-based and reinforcement-learning MAPF solvers is left for future work. © 2026 SPIE.

title: Integrating Digital Twins and MAS for Scalable AGV Fleet Management in Smart Warehousing
authors: Wouters, Liam; Alvarado, Victor Pena; Van Loon, Richard; Khalilipour, Alireza; Challenger, Moharram
venue: 2026 15th Mediterranean Conference on Embedded Computing, MECO 2026 - Proceedings
abstract: The growing demand for efficiency, scalability, and safety in smart warehousing requires advanced coordination mechanisms for autonomous robotic fleets operating in cyber-physical environments. This paper presents a digital twin-driven, scalable cyber-physical architecture for automated guided vehicle (AGV) fleet management. The framework centers on a centralized digital twin that provides global system awareness, predictive path planning, and high-level coordination, while physical robots execute tasks in a distributed manner. The digital twin integrates a multi-agent coordination layer with a simulation environment, enabling real-time synchronization between physical and virtual components via OPC UA. A JADE-based multi-agent system enables decentralized agent interaction, while the digital twin supports environment-aware decision-making, dynamic task allocation, and collision risk prediction. The architecture incorporates adaptive scheduling, battery-aware task management, and static and dynamic collision avoidance, all coordinated through priority-based coordination. A proof-of-concept implementation using LEGO-based AGVs, Ultra Wideband localization, and a simulation-driven digital twin environment demonstrates the approach's feasibility. Experimental observations demonstrate improved coordination efficiency, operational safety, and scalability in dynamic warehouse environments. The results highlight the effectiveness of integrating centralized digital twin intelligence with distributed multi-agent execution for next-generation smart warehousing systems. © 2026 IEEE.

title: ATLASky-AI: An autonomous framework for physics-based trustworthy verification of LLM-generated spatiotemporal knowledge
authors: Awill, Raed; Khan, Wajahat Ali; Hussain, Maqbool; Anderson, Ben; Kazmi, S. M Ahsan
venue: Expert Systems with Applications
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to revolutionize knowledge extraction from unstructured data in systems that track physical entities through spacetime, but their tendency to hallucinate (generating plausible but false information) renders them too risky for deployment in safety-critical domains. Prior verification methods are caught in a circular dependency, requiring the ground-truth labels they aim to produce, validating spatial and temporal dimensions independently rather than concurrently, and suffering catastrophic accuracy degradation under distribution shift. To address these limitations, we introduce ATLASky-AI, an autonomous trustworthy AI framework for verifying LLM-generated facts in 4D Spatiotemporal Knowledge Graphs used across safety-critical domains including digital twins, healthcare tracking systems, manufacturing, and logistics. The framework makes real-time verification decisions autonomously using intrinsic quality metrics, eliminating the need for instance-level labeled ground truth during runtime inference. An adaptive monitoring system leverages sparse expert feedback (0.3% sampling) to maintain high accuracy over time under distribution drift. The core architecture orchestrates five specialized verification modules targeting distinct error patterns: ontology validation, standards compliance, physics-based spatiotemporal constraint checking, external source corroboration, and statistical anomaly detection. Evaluated across aerospace and healthcare datasets, ATLASky-AI achieves an average of 94% precision and 93% recall, with false positive rates of just 2.6–4.1%. This represents a 39–57% reduction compared to the best baseline system. A six-month pilot deployment at an aerospace manufacturing company, AddQual Ltd., validates its practical impact, demonstrating a 99.8% reduction in knowledge graph creation time (from 48 h to 4.2 min) and a 3.5-month return on investment. These results establish ATLASky-AI as an effective trustworthy AI solution, enabling safe integration of LLMs with mission-critical systems requiring spatiotemporal knowledge validation. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC license. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

title: CTS-CBS: A New Approach for Multiagent Collaborative Task Sequencing and Path Finding
authors: Jiang, Junkai; Li, Ruochen; Yang, Yibin; Chen, Yihe; Wang, Yuning; Xu, Shaobing; Wang, Jianqiang
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
abstract: This article addresses a generalization problem of multiagent pathfinding (MAPF), called collaborative task sequencing - MAPF (CTS-MAPF), where agents must plan collision-free paths and visit a series of intermediate task locations in an optimized order before reaching their final destinations. To address this problem, we propose a new approach, collaborative task sequencing - conflict-based search (CTS-CBS), which conducts a two-level search. At the high level, it generates a search forest, where each tree corresponds to a joint task sequence derived from the joint-traveling salesman problem (jTSP) solution. At the low level, CTS-CBS performs constrained single-agent path planning to generate paths for each agent while adhering to high-level constraints. Furthermore, we integrate explicit estimation search (EES) into CTS-CBS to enhance the search efficiency. We also provide theoretical guarantees of its solution completeness and optimality (or suboptimality with a bounded parameter). To evaluate the performance of CTS-CBS, we utilize three datasets with different map sizes, map difficulty, and agent/task numbers, and conduct comprehensive experiments. The results show that our algorithms demonstrate significant improvements in success rate and runtime, while maintaining competitive solution quality. Finally, practical robot simulation and tests demonstrate the algorithm's applicability in real-world scenarios. © 2014 IEEE.

title: LLM-assisted quality-aware GA–multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient framework for multi-robot collaborative scheduling in construction quality control
authors: Zhu, Meihao; Liu, Zhansheng; Zhou, Hao; Li, Weiyi; Wang, Song; Zhang, Qingwen
venue: Automation in Construction
abstract: Multi-robot construction quality control often suffers from limited adaptability, expensive quality-aware scheduling evaluation, and unstable cooperative execution. This paper proposes an Improved-GA-MADDPG-LLM framework that integrates scheduling optimization, multi-agent execution, and semantic quality feedback.
